Plan: `memory-pg-lexical-own-injection-2026-07-13`. Owner mandate: the lexical
leg must be papercusp code over papercusp storage, and ambient injection must
be papercusp-controlled — no dependency on Claude's file-memory implementation.

## Update 2026-07-28 — hybrid-pg is now the DEFAULT, and the ~/.claude backends are gone

`memory-declaude-and-defaults-2026-07-28` finished the job this plan started. Three
changes to what is written below:

* **`hybrid-pg` is the default backend**, not `mem0` — `DEFAULT_MEMORY_BACKEND` in
  `backend-selection.ts`. Until then a fresh install silently got the 53%-recall
  backend, and the 98% one was reachable only by knowing to flip a dropdown.
* **`claude-file` and `hybrid` are NO LONGER REGISTERED** and cannot be selected.
  The "Cutover / rollback" section below says the old `hybrid` "stays registered as
  the rollback" — that is no longer true, and deliberately so: rolling back onto a
  frozen file store is not a rollback, it is a data-visibility regression. The
  rollback for `hybrid-pg` is `mem0` (same rows, cosine leg only).
  ⚠ A persisted `memory_backend` row or `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_BACKEND` still naming a
  retired backend is **coerced to the default with a one-time warning** rather than
  throwing `unknown memory backend` on every call — `RETIRED_MEMORY_BACKENDS` in
  `backend-selection.ts`. Unregistering a backend without that coercion is a live
  outage for anyone who had legitimately selected it.
* **`HybridBackend` takes its `name` from options** instead of hardcoding `'hybrid'`.
  The canary's flip-reseed guard below (`set.backend !== backend.name`) compares
  exactly that string, so while both wirings answered `'hybrid'` a flip between them
  skipped the reseed and scored against a baseline from the *other* backend.
* The settings page's stale "Memory index over capacity" banner (which counted
  ~/.claude topic files and told you to curate them, ~2 weeks after the generator
  that consumed them was retired) is deleted, along with `claude-hygiene.ts` — the
  last unconditional ~/.claude read in the operator.

`ClaudeFileMemoryBackend` still exists as a lib class: the offline bench constructs
it directly to reproduce the A/B numbers below. It is unreachable from the product.

## The shape

**One canonical store**: `harness_shared.memory_canonical` (payload jsonb) +
one `memory_vec_<mode>` table per embedding space (`vec-write.ts` `VEC_TABLE` /
`MODE_DIMS` are the single source of truth for that set — derive from them,
never hand-copy the list).

**Two recall legs, same rows** (`hybrid-pg`, registered in `configure.ts`):

- **Cosine leg** — `Mem0Backend.search`: pgvector distance over the active
  embedder mode's vec table, per-scope fan-out, decay + diversity rerank.
- **Lexical leg** — `Mem0Backend.searchLexical` →
  `CanonicalVectorStore.lexicalSearch`: embed-free, field-weighted token match
  (`payload->>'name'` ×3 > `'description'` ×2 > `'data'` ×1, normalized by
  tokens×3 — parity with the claude-file scoring that benched best on
  exact-identifier recall), min-2-char identifier-preserving tokenizer
  (`lexicalTokens`, which emits a compound like `PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_TIMEOUT` whole
  *and* its `_`/`-` subtokens). **The score is computed IN SQL and the `ORDER BY`
  is the score** — see the ranking trap below.
- Fusion: `HybridBackend` RRF (floored-union). Both legs return the SAME
  canonical ids, so fusion dedupes by construction.

`LexicalLegBackend` (`lexical-leg.ts`) presents the lexical capability as a
standalone `MemoryBackend` for the hybrid's constructor. **Its `remember()` is
a deliberate no-op** — `HybridBackend.remember` write-through-projects into
its lexical leg, which is correct for two SEPARATE stores (the old `hybrid`:
claude topic files + PG) but would double-write when both legs share
`memory_canonical`.

## Why (the evidence)

- Frozen-corpus bench: lexical wins exact-identifier recall (MRR 0.99 vs 0.87
  cosine); cosine wins paraphrase. Complementary failure modes → hybrid.
- Live A/B (2026-07-13, 40 known-item pairs from post-June memories,
  `bench/ab-live-recall-cli.ts`, **post-token-cap-fix**):

  | backend | recall@10 (admitted) | retrieval@10 | p50 |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | mem0 | 21/40 (53%) | 63% | 1023ms |
  | old `hybrid` | 22/40 (55%) | 63% | 1061ms |
  | **`hybrid-pg`** | **39/40 (98%)** | **100%** | 1288ms |

  The old hybrid's file leg only saw write-through projections; the PG lexical
  leg sees every canonical row. **Read the p50 honestly**: hybrid-pg is the
  *slowest* of the three (+21% over hybrid), not the fastest — it buys ~78% more
  recall for that. An earlier draft of this page cited 83% recall and "p50 816ms
  (fastest)"; those were **pre-fix** numbers measured while `LEXICAL_MAX_TOKENS`
  was still mangling long queries (see the cap trap below) — they are superseded,
  and the speed claim did not survive.

## The latency fix: an indexable pre-filter + concurrent legs (EI-10931)

Two independent bugs made `hybrid-pg` slower than the backend it replaces
(bench p50 1182ms vs 821ms). Both are fixed; both are worth knowing, because
each is a trap that reads as a virtue.

### 1. The score expression WAS the filter — so no index could ever be used

Every ILIKE lived in the **SELECT list** (the field-weighted `CASE` score), and
`lex_raw > 0` was applied in an **outer** query. The inner scan's only predicate
was `invalid_at IS NULL` — so Postgres read and **scored every row**, every
search:

```
Seq Scan on memory_canonical (actual time=1.368..774.428 rows=1287 loops=1)
Execution Time: 775.674 ms          -- 13,594 active rows, 12-token query
```

This was *deliberate*, and the code said so: "each ILIKE is evaluated exactly
once: the score expression IS the filter, so there is no separate OR pre-filter."
It saves re-evaluating a handful of ILIKEs on the few rows that match — at the
cost of a **full scan on every single search, forever, growing with the store.**

⚠ **The trap for the next person: adding a `pg_trgm` GIN index alone does
NOTHING here.** There is no predicate for it to serve. (An earlier version of this
page recommended exactly that — it was wrong, and it would have been a day
wasted staring at an index the planner never touches.) The index only works
*together with* an indexable `WHERE`.

The fix is both halves: `lexicalSearch` now also emits an **OR pre-filter** into
the inner `WHERE` (`name/description/data ILIKE $t OR …` across the tokens), which
is **logically identical** to `lex_raw > 0` — a row scores > 0 iff ≥1 token hits ≥1
field — so **recall cannot change by construction**; only the plan changes. Plus
migration **594**: `pg_trgm` + GIN `gin_trgm_ops` indexes on the three payload
expressions.

Result — the plan flips to a `BitmapOr` over the trigram indexes:

| query class | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **rare identifier** (this leg's whole purpose) | 775ms | **1.2ms** |
| broad common-token paraphrase | 776ms | ~630ms |

Common tokens genuinely match ~9.5% of the store (1287 rows), and each survivor
still re-ILIKEs a large `data` field — an index cannot shrink a candidate set that
is really that big. That residue is what fix #2 hides.

⚠ **Still do NOT reach for a weighted `tsvector`.** It looks like the perfect fit
(`setweight` A/B/D maps straight onto the 3/2/1 weights) — but
`to_tsvector('english', …)` stems and drops stop-words, which **mangles
identifiers** (`PAPERCUSP_MEMORY_TIMEOUT`, `WI-4522`, camelCase tool names).
Exact-identifier recall is the entire reason this leg exists (MRR 1.00 vs cosine's
0.87), so a tsvector migration would silently destroy its purpose while looking
like a clean optimization. `gin_trgm_ops` accelerates `ILIKE '%x%'` with *identical*
semantics — no stemming, no tokenization change, no recall risk.

### 2. The two legs ran SERIALLY

`HybridBackend.search` did `await cosine` **then** `await lexical`. The legs are
**independent** — two rankings of the same rows, neither's input depending on the
other's output — so sequencing them put the lexical leg's whole cost on the
critical path: `total = cosine + lexical` instead of `max(cosine, lexical)`.

That was free to ignore while the lexical leg was a local file scan (~0ms). It
became the **dominant** term the moment the leg became a PG query. The cosine leg
is embed-bound (a network round-trip); the lexical leg is embed-free and DB-bound.
Overlapping them hides the cheaper one entirely behind the one we cannot avoid.

Floored-union mode (the default, and what `hybrid-pg` runs) now starts the lexical
leg **before** awaiting cosine. ⚠ `cosine-gated` mode still short-circuits
deliberately — an empty cosine set must skip the lexical work entirely — and a test
pins that contract (*"cosine-gated early-return short-circuits the lexical leg
entirely"*). The first cut of this fix broke it; the suite caught it.

Guard: `hybrid-backend.test.ts` → *"floored-union runs BOTH legs concurrently"*
asserts the lexical leg is **started before cosine resolves**. A refactor that
innocently rewrites it back to `await; await;` would restore the regression with
every other test still green.

## ~/.claude topic files are NOT load-bearing anymore

- All pre-existing topic-file memories were imported into the canonical store
  (`claude-import-cli.ts`, P-004): 71 net-new of 1,806 active files — 1,630
  were already write-through projections (`extra.link_id` = the canonical id),
  26 were ghosts of canonical deletes (deliberately NOT resurrected), 79 exact
  dups. `archive/` was excluded (plan D-005 — evictions stay evicted; backup
  tar at `~/.papercusp/backups/p004-memory-import/`).
- Idempotency: imported rows carry `payload.imported_from =
  'claude-file:<basename>'`; re-runs no-op.
- `MEMORY.md` is now a static **pointer stub** (P-008), and the
  `memory-compact.mjs` SessionStart generator that used to rebuild it is retired
  to `~/.claude/scripts/retired/` (P-009). Ambient recall is papercusp-owned: the
  MCP initialize prelude (`mcp-prelude.ts`), `coord:orient` memory folds,
  work-item claim injection, and the post-compaction re-prime.
- ⚠ **The generator had already stopped running before we retired it** — its hook
  wiring was silently dropped by the 2026-07-12 managed-hooks migration, and
  *nothing alarmed*. `MEMORY.md` sat frozen for weeks while still advertising
  itself as "AUTO-GENERATED … regenerated at each session start" — a stale
  snapshot confidently presenting itself as current. It was found by accident.
  The missing **detector** (a liveness assertion on each declared hook's
  last-fire) is the real defect and is filed as **EI-10907**; retiring the files
  only removed this one instance.

## Cutover / rollback

- The switch is the persisted `memory_backend` operator setting
  (`backend-selection.ts`, 15s SWR so all processes converge without
  restarts). `hybrid-pg` ↔ `hybrid` is runtime-reversible; the old `hybrid`
  stays registered as the rollback.
- ⚠ A process running code WITHOUT the `hybrid-pg` registration throws
  `unknown memory backend` on every memory call if the setting is flipped
  early — deploy the code first, flip second.
- Watchdogs: the live recall canary (`recall-canary.ts`, EI-10047) auto-reseeds
  its pair set on a backend flip, and its P-010 probe measures the LEXICAL leg
  separately every run — a blind leg (zero lexical retrieval while the fused
  product serves rows) alarms as `degraded` even when cosine carries recall.

## Traps this replaced (don't re-learn them)

- **Never rank a lexical candidate pool by RECENCY and then score it.** The first
  cut of `lexicalSearch` pulled `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT max(topK*5, 50)`
  and did the field-weighted scoring in JS over the survivors. That truncates the
  pool *before* anything is scored, so the best lexical match is dropped without
  ever being scored whenever it loses a recency race to rows that merely share a
  common word. It cost lexical-gap MRR on the frozen bench (0.68 vs the file leg's
  0.75 — the paraphrase queries reach their answer only through a couple of generic
  words), and on a live store it silently breaks **exact-identifier recall**, which
  is the whole reason this leg exists: a rare identifier sitting in an old row never
  enters the candidate pool at all. A small bench corpus HIDES this — with 114 rows a
  cap of 50 still admits most of the corpus. The fix is structural: the per-token
  `CASE` weights are computed in SQL, `WHERE lex_raw > 0 ORDER BY lex_raw DESC LIMIT
  topK` — ranking over the whole matching set, each ILIKE evaluated once (the score
  expression *is* the filter). Guard:
  `canonical-lexical-search.integration.test.ts` → "ranks an OLD strong match above
  many NEWER weak ones" (60 newer common-word rows vs one old identifier row), which
  fails if a recency-ordered candidate cap is ever reintroduced.
- **A cap is a SAFETY bound on pathological input — never a relevance knob.**
  `LEXICAL_MAX_TOKENS` was `12`, while real recall queries run ~20 tokens
  (gold-set v1: p50 10, **p95 24, max 28**). So the cap silently discarded ~40%
  of every long query — and it discarded the *tail*, which is where the
  discriminative terms live (a paraphrase query front-loads common words and
  reaches its answer through the rare ones at the end). Worse, the score was
  then normalized by the **truncated** token count, so a mangled query still
  looked confidently scored. Measured on the lexical leg alone (lexical-gap
  MRR): cap 12 → **0.432**, 16 → 0.428, 24 → 0.544, 32 → **0.546**, uncapped →
  0.546 (the claude-file leg: 0.552). Fixed at 32 — comfortably above p95, still
  a real bound on a runaway input.
  **Why it hid for two whole diagnostic rounds:** *exact-identifier MRR is 1.000
  at EVERY cap* — those queries are short, so they never hit it. Only the
  paraphrase class regressed, which made a **tokenizer** bug present as a
  *fusion/ranking* bug, and sent two plausible ranking "fixes" through the
  acceptance gate before the real cause was isolated. When one query class
  regresses and another is untouched, suspect the INPUT PATH the two classes
  don't share (here: query length) before you re-litigate the scorer. Guard:
  `canonical-store.test.ts` → "does NOT truncate a real natural-language query"
  (a 28-token query must survive intact).
- The bench's isolated `bench_memory` schema used to hand-mirror production
  DDL and drifted TWICE in one day (missing `memory_vec_harrier`, then missing
  the temporal-lite columns) — every PG backend benched at literal zero
  (EI-10793). `ensureBenchSchema` now clones live tables
  (`LIKE harness_shared.* INCLUDING ALL`), and **drops + recreates at run
  START** — a killed run used to leave rows behind that contaminated the next
  run's corpus (and two concurrently-launched runs cross-seeded the same schema,
  garbaging both; EI-10854).
- Unscoped topic files used to surface under ANY scope via the claude-file
  backend's visibility-first trick. The import maps them to the OWNER'S USER
  POOL because the live `memory:search` fan-out queries
  `[user.id, harness:*…]` — never `'local'`.
